design_detail: Coordinate-based voxel-wise meta-analysis (Seed-based d Mapping with Permutation of Subject Images, SDM-PSI version 6.11) of functional neuroimaging studies that scanned healthy volunteers during acute ketamine administration against placebo or a baseline condition. Three whole-brain analyses were run: resting-state studies (10), task-based studies across all cognitive domains (23), and the subset of task studies using executive-function and verbal-fluency tasks (9). Maps were built at an uncorrected voxel threshold of z > 2.5 with a cluster extent above 20 voxels, and also reported after family-wise correction by threshold-free cluster enhancement (TFCE, 1000 permutations, corrected p < .05). Heterogeneity (I-squared) and Egger's regression tests were computed for each significant cluster, and meta-regressions and sub-analyses tested moderators (pp. 212-214).
can_establish: Where, across the published coordinates of small ketamine-challenge imaging studies in healthy volunteers, increased activation converges: one cluster in the dorsal anterior cingulate at rest and one in the right Heschl's gyrus during executive-function tasks survive correction, with three smaller clusters below it.
cannot_establish: The size of any effect (coordinate-based meta-analysis recovers no interpretable effect estimate or confidence interval); any decrease in activation (none was found and absence of a cluster is not evidence of no change); anything about connectivity or about regions of interest (both were excluded by design); the behaviour of the default-mode network as such (no deactivation contrast was analysed); dose, ketamine type or plasma-level dependence (all moderator tests were null in 10 and 9 studies, which is far too few to exclude moderation); the quality of the primary studies (no risk-of-bias assessment was done); and anything about people with depression, schizophrenia or repeated dosing (all excluded or absent).

sample.recruitment: Database search of PubMed and Web of Science in September 2021 with a single Boolean string combining neuroimaging terms with ketamine, plus the same query in Google Scholar and cross-referencing (p. 212). The initial search yielded 876 articles with 11 more found through reference lists; 808 abstracts were excluded, 79 full texts screened, 46 excluded and 33 retained (p. 214). Participants in the pooled studies are healthy volunteers in academic imaging laboratories, mostly men.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: original peer-reviewed articles; healthy participants free of any psychiatric disorder; measurement of acute brain activity during ketamine exposure; fMRI (including arterial spin labelling) or PET; a measure of blood-oxygen-level-dependent signal, regional cerebral blood flow, glucose metabolism or fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations; measurement at rest or during a task; and whole-brain analysis. Excluded: studies of psychiatric populations, functional connectivity studies (because of the heterogeneity of analytical approaches) and studies confined to a small number of a priori regions of interest (pp. 212-213). No language or date limit is stated.
sample.demographics: Resting-state studies: 198 participants by the paper's count, 75% male, mean age 27.71 years; three used racemic ketamine, two S-ketamine and five did not specify; eight assessed psychotomimetic symptoms explicitly; eight were fMRI and two PET; seven were within-person and three between-group designs; three used a baseline rather than a placebo condition (Table 1, p. 214; Results, p. 214). Task-activation studies: 371 participants, 72% male, mean age 27.4 years; 12 racemic, 7 S-ketamine, 4 unspecified; 21 assessed psychotomimetic symptoms; study sizes run from 8 to 27 participants (Table 2, p. 215; Results, p. 214).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; attrition within the primary studies is neither extracted nor reported.
sample.selection_effects: Two databases and Google Scholar, one search string, no grey literature, no trial or study registries, no contact with authors, and a search run in September 2021 for an article accepted in February 2023. Only studies reporting whole-brain coordinates can enter a coordinate-based meta-analysis, so studies that reported only regions of interest or only connectivity are excluded by design and studies with no significant whole-brain peak contribute little; the pooled literature is therefore the published, whole-brain, peak-reporting subset. Individual studies are small (5 to 34 participants) and predominantly male.

exposure.measurement: Ketamine was given in the laboratory in every primary study; the review extracted dose, ketamine type and route of administration, and tabulated ketamine type and mean plasma level, but not dose, which is held in supplementary tables S1 and S2 that were not read (pp. 212, 214). Of the 19 studies in the two analyses that produced results, 8 reported a plasma level explicitly: mean 98.08 ng/mL, printed as plus or minus 37.68, range 16.6 to 183 (p. 219).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as the review describes them: intravenous administration, with the introduction citing bolus doses of 0.1 to 0.26 mg/kg and infusion doses of 0.25 to 0.72 mg/kg per hour as the range that produces psychotomimetic effects (p. 211), and the discussion stating that all doses in the included studies lay within the therapeutic antidepressant range, on average 0.5 mg/kg over 40 minutes, range 0.1 to 0.75 mg/kg (p. 218). Scanning was during acute administration only; no study gave repeated doses. Racemic ketamine in 15 studies, S-ketamine in 9, unspecified in 9 (Tables 1 and 2, pp. 214-215).
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable as a confounder at review level: participants were healthy volunteers free of psychiatric disorder, and the primary studies' criteria for other drug use were not extracted or reported. One included study (Rowland et al., 2010) examined ketamine together with nicotine.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; all measurements were made during acute administration, and the review states that no included study exposed participants to prolonged ketamine administration (p. 219).

comparison.controls: Within each primary study, the same participants scanned under placebo or at baseline (7 of 10 resting-state studies were within-person; 3 of 10 compared separate groups, contributing the 59 participants of the second column of Table 1), or, in three resting-state studies, a baseline condition with no placebo (Table 1, p. 214).
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level. Whether the control condition was placebo or baseline was tested as a moderator in the resting-state analysis and was not significant (pp. 213, 214-215).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable: the exposure is an administered drug, not a history of use. What is unmeasured is anything about the people who were scanned beyond age and sex ratio, and about the primary studies beyond the columns of Tables 1 and 2.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not reported; the review did not extract the primary studies' exclusion criteria for other substances.

outcomes.instruments: Brain activation during ketamine relative to placebo or baseline, as peak coordinates and t-values reported by each primary study and re-imputed by SDM-PSI into effect-size maps (Hedges' effect size) pooled in a random-effects model allowing for sample size, intra-study variability and between-study heterogeneity, with multiple imputations pooled by Rubin's rules and family-wise error assessed by a subject-based permutation test (pp. 213). Signals pooled together: blood-oxygen-level-dependent fMRI, arterial spin labelling and PET cerebral blood flow, PET glucose metabolism, and fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations. Tasks were classified into cognitive domains using the classification from the team's earlier meta-analyses of cognition in substance use (p. 212); the executive-function pool combines verbal fluency, working memory and related tasks (Results, p. 214; Table 2, p. 215).
outcomes.validity_norms: No appraisal of the primary studies was made with any instrument, and none of their imaging-analysis choices (smoothing, thresholding, correction) is recorded. The review notes the field-wide problem of inflated false-positive rates in cluster inference by citing Eklund-type work on cluster failure (p. 213) but does not assess it in the included studies. Whether each study reported psychotomimetic symptoms, and whether task performance was poorer under ketamine, are tabulated as yes/no/not specified, not as measured scores.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Ketamine-induced activation' is a cluster where the pooled imputed effect of ketamine relative to the control condition exceeds the threshold. Two thresholds are reported throughout: an uncorrected voxel threshold of z > 2.5 with more than 20 voxels, and TFCE correction at p < .05, which only one cluster in each of two analyses survived. The abstract, discussion and conclusions carry both, labelled.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Within each whole-brain map, family-wise error was controlled by a subject-based permutation test with TFCE (1000 permutations, corrected p < .05); uncorrected maps (z > 2.5, cluster > 20 voxels) are also reported and are the basis of three of the five clusters named in the abstract. Editors' count of 16: three whole-brain analyses (resting-state, all task domains, executive-function tasks), each testing increases and decreases, plus about 13 moderator analyses (roughly 8 for resting-state and 5 for executive functions). No correction was applied across the three analyses or across the moderator tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Screening and inclusion were decided by two authors by consensus (p. 212); data extraction was done by two authors according to the author-contribution statement (p. 220), with no statement that it was duplicated or checked.

analysis.effect_sizes: No interpretable effect estimates are reported: SDM-PSI output is given as peak MNI coordinates, a Z-value, a p-value and a cluster size, with no Hedges' g per cluster, no confidence intervals and no prediction intervals (Table 3, p. 216). Resting state, ketamine greater than placebo: left anterior cingulate and paracingulate gyri, BA 24, at 0; 30; 20, Z = 4.265, p < 0.001, 658 voxels, the only cluster to survive TFCE correction (495 voxels in the table footnote, 496 in the text); right insula, BA 47, at 36; 24; -6, Z = 3.432, p < 0.001, 30 voxels; right fusiform gyrus, BA 30, at 22; -34; -16, Z = 2.933, p < 0.002, 26 voxels. Executive-function tasks, ketamine greater than control: right Heschl's gyrus, BA 48, at 44; -16; 6, Z = 3.306, p < 0.001, 160 voxels, surviving TFCE with 142 voxels, with the cluster breakdown naming the right insula and right Heschl's gyrus; right anterior cingulate and paracingulate gyri, BA 10, at 6; 52; 8, Z = 2.889, p < 0.002, 26 voxels. Across all task domains together, no cluster of increased or decreased activation reached significance, and no decrease was significant in any analysis. Heterogeneity was between 0.15% and 6.45% for all results and Egger's tests gave all p-values above 0.24 (p. 214).
analysis.covariates: None at review level. Moderators were tested one at a time by meta-regression or sub-analysis: for resting-state studies age, sex ratio, dose (bolus and infusion), imaging modality, signal measured, control condition and presence of psychotic-like symptoms, all null; for the executive-function studies age, sex ratio, ketamine type, psychotic-like symptoms and task impairment, all null (pp. 214-215; supplementary tables S3 and S4 were not read).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned anywhere; the review states that PRISMA reporting guidelines were followed (p. 213). No PROSPERO record is cited.
analysis.selective_reporting: The analyses reported match those announced, and both corrected and uncorrected results are labelled throughout. Two gaps: the moderator set named in the Methods for resting-state studies includes ketamine type and omits dose, while the Results report dose and omit ketamine type; and the numbers that bear on strength of evidence (dose per study, I-squared per cluster beyond a range, Egger's p per cluster) are given only as ranges or deferred to supplements.
analysis.power: Not formally addressed; the paper names its small sample as its first limitation (n = 628 in all; n = 395 in the two analyses that yielded results) and says the number of studies limited the power to detect major differences and prevented analyses of episodic memory, social cognition and emotion processing (p. 219). With 10 and 9 studies, the moderator analyses and the Egger's tests have very little power, so their null results cannot be read as evidence of no moderation or no publication bias.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Pooling the published whole-brain coordinates of small ketamine-challenge studies in healthy volunteers, two clusters of increased activation survive correction: the dorsal anterior cingulate at rest (658 voxels uncorrected, 495 after TFCE) and the right Heschl's gyrus extending into the posterior insula during executive-function tasks (160 voxels, 142 after TFCE). Three further clusters (right insula 30 voxels, right fusiform gyrus 26 voxels, rostral anterior cingulate 26 voxels) appear only at an uncorrected threshold. Across the 23 task studies taken together nothing was significant, and no decrease in activation was found anywhere. Moderator analyses, all in 9 or 10 studies, were null.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The conclusions state that the results show ketamine disrupts the salience network at rest and that it activates task-irrelevant regions during executive functions while preventing the deactivation of the task-negative default-mode network (p. 219); the abstract says the findings are coherent with alterations found in schizophrenia, which it says confer external validity on the ketamine model of psychosis (p. 211). Four gaps. (1) The default-mode claim rests on the 26-voxel uncorrected rostral anterior cingulate cluster, which the discussion itself calls weak and not to be overinterpreted (p. 219); no deactivation contrast was analysed, so a failure to deactivate is an inference from an increase, not a measured quantity. (2) The salience-network claim rests on one corrected anterior cingulate cluster plus the 30-voxel uncorrected insula cluster, about which the paper separately warns against over-interpretation (p. 218). (3) The legends of both figures describe the regions as having been impaired by ketamine, when every result in Table 3 is an increase in activation, and two panels are drawn at a lowered threshold to improve the picture. (4) Near-zero heterogeneity and null Egger's tests are reported without noting that with 9 or 10 studies neither is informative. Against this, the abstract separates corrected from uncorrected results, the discussion is repeatedly cautious about the small clusters, and the conclusions call the meta-analysis preliminary.

timeline.event: Krystal et al. establish the acute psychotomimetic, perceptual and cognitive profile of subanesthetic ketamine in healthy volunteers, the basis of the model this review tests
Lahti et al. show the acute symptom-provoking effect in people with schizophrenia

Beck et al., systematic review and meta-analysis of ketamine-induced psychiatric symptoms, cited by this review as the basis for calling ketamine a valid model of psychosis (JAMA Network Open; on the project's list, not yet appraised)

Kotoula et al., systematic review of resting-state connectivity after subanesthetic ketamine in healthy and depressed people, covering the connectivity literature this review excludes (cited at p. 212)

Simon et al., meta-analysis from the same research team of the acute cognitive effects of ketamine and esketamine in healthy volunteers, used here to interpret the executive-function finding (cited at pp. 212, 218-219)
This review: by its authors' account the first meta-analysis of ketamine-induced brain activity at rest and during task in healthy participants (p. 215)

replication.where_it_stands: The only coordinate-based meta-analysis of this literature identified by its authors. It is best read as a map of where the published peaks converge, not as a measurement: two corrected clusters, three uncorrected ones, no decreases, and null moderator tests in 9 to 10 studies. Claims should carry the thresholds with the findings, should not cite the insula, fusiform or rostral anterior cingulate clusters without saying they are uncorrected, and should not use this source for connectivity, for effect sizes, or for anything about people with depression or psychotic illness.

funding.funder: The paper states that the authors reported no funding associated with the work (p. 220).
funding.declared_conflicts: The disclosure statement reads that no potential conflict of interest was reported by the authors (p. 219).
funding.affiliations_note: Centre de recherche de l'Institut Universitaire en Sante Mentale de Montreal and Department of psychiatry and addiction, Universite de Montreal (p. 211). The acknowledgments state that the senior author holds the Eli Lilly Canada Chair on schizophrenia research and that the second author holds a master's scholarship from the Fonds de Recherche du Quebec en Sante (p. 219), so a named industry chair appears in the acknowledgments while the disclosure statement reports no conflict. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results. The review also relies on the team's own earlier meta-analyses for its task classification and for interpreting the cognitive findings.

what_would_settle_it: An image-based meta-analysis or mega-analysis of the original statistical maps rather than peak coordinates, from a pre-registered consortium of ketamine-challenge studies using a common infusion protocol with plasma sampling, scanning both rest and a fixed executive task, reporting activation and deactivation contrasts with effect sizes and confidence intervals at a single pre-specified threshold, powered to test dose and ketamine type as moderators, and appraising the risk of bias of each contributing dataset.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (healthy volunteers free of psychiatric disorder), intervention (acute ketamine), comparator (placebo or baseline) and outcome (whole-brain activation, at rest or during a task) are all specified in the selection criteria (pp. 212-213).
No protocol, registration number or a priori analysis plan is mentioned; only adherence to PRISMA reporting is stated (p. 213).

The criteria name what was admitted and give a reason for excluding connectivity studies, but no rationale is given for the design restriction itself; within-person and between-group studies are pooled together, with design recorded in Table 1 and never discussed.

Two databases plus Google Scholar, with the Boolean string printed, and cross-referencing of reference lists, within 24 months of acceptance; but no grey literature, no trial or study registries, no contact with experts or authors, and a single generic search string with no subject headings or filters reported (p. 212).
Two authors reviewed the studies and decided inclusion by consensus against the stated criteria (p. 212).

The Methods list what was extracted but not by whom or in duplicate; the author-contribution statement says two authors did data extraction (p. 220), which does not establish independent duplicate extraction or consensus on the extracted data.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The article gives counts only (808 abstracts excluded, 46 full texts excluded) and refers to Supplementary Figure S1 for the latter; whether that figure or another supplement lists the excluded full texts with reasons can be judged only from the supplementary material, which was not read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Tables 1 and 2 give per-study n, mean age, sex ratio, ketamine type, mean plasma level, whether psychotomimetic symptoms were assessed, imaging modality, signal, control condition, design and task type; but dose is deferred to supplements, and the setting, country, timing of scanning relative to dosing and participant selection criteria of each study are absent (pp. 214-215).

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No risk-of-bias assessment of any kind was made, with no instrument named and no appraisal of blinding, analysis choices, thresholding or selective reporting in the primary studies.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: SDM-PSI 6.11 with multiple imputation of effect-size maps, a random-effects model allowing for sample size, intra-study variance and between-study heterogeneity, Rubin's rules for pooling imputations and a subject-based permutation test with TFCE for family-wise error is the appropriate current method for coordinate-based meta-analysis, and both corrected and uncorrected results are labelled (p. 213). Weaknesses the item does not score: within-person and between-group designs, and four signal types, are pooled in each map, and the uncorrected clusters are carried into the abstract and conclusions.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No analysis of the effect of study quality on the pooled maps, because no risk of bias was assessed; the moderator analyses concern dose, type, modality, signal and sample characteristics, not study quality.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The discussion is cautious about cluster size and about the small number of studies and acknowledges inflated false-positive rates in cluster inference as a field-wide problem (p. 213), but no judgment about the risk of bias of the included studies enters the interpretation, since none was made.

I-squared is reported for the significant results as a range (0.15% to 6.45%), the convention of I-squared above 50% is stated, and the variability of ketamine type, dose and plasma level across studies is discussed at length in the limitations and tested by meta-regression (pp. 213-214, 219). The near-zero values are not themselves interrogated.

Egger's regression tests were run for each significant cluster, with all p-values above 0.24 (pp. 213-214). With 9 or 10 studies these tests have very little power, which the paper does not note; and coordinate-based meta-analysis can only include studies that published whole-brain peaks.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: A funding statement (none) and a disclosure statement (no conflict) are both printed (pp. 219-220); the senior author's named industry chair appears in the acknowledgments rather than in the disclosure.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 7 is recorded as no information because whether the excluded full texts are listed with reasons can be judged only from supplementary material that was not read, so this overall rating is provisional in the sense of METHODS 5.3. Even so, the rating does not depend on it: three critical items are met at best partly or not at all (item 2, no protocol; item 4, partial; item 9, no appraisal of the primary studies) and item 13 follows item 9, which is more than one critical flaw and gives critically low confidence. This is a judgment about how far the pooled maps can be trusted as unbiased summaries, not about the paper's care: the statistical method is the appropriate one, corrected and uncorrected results are kept apart, publication bias was tested, and the authors call their own work preliminary. The practical consequences are that the primary studies' quality is unknown and unweighted, that two of the five named clusters in the abstract and three of five overall survive only an uncorrected threshold, and that with 9 to 10 small studies the null moderator and publication-bias tests carry almost no information. The source can be cited for where increased activation converges across these studies, with its thresholds attached, and for the descriptive composition of the literature (study counts, sample sizes, ketamine types, plasma levels, how many studies assessed psychotomimetic symptoms). It cannot be cited for effect sizes, for decreases in activation, for connectivity, for default-mode deactivation, for dose-response, or for people who are not healthy volunteers.

key_findings.finding: At rest, ketamine increased activation in the left anterior cingulate and paracingulate gyri (BA 24; MNI 0; 30; 20; Z = 4.265; p < 0.001; 658 voxels), the only cluster to survive TFCE correction (495 voxels in the table footnote, given as 496 in the text). Two further clusters appeared only at the uncorrected threshold: right insula (BA 47; 36; 24; -6; Z = 3.432; p < 0.001; 30 voxels) and right fusiform gyrus (BA 30; 22; -34; -16; Z = 2.933; p < 0.002; 26 voxels).
key_findings.locator: Results > Meta-analysis of resting-state activity (p. 214); Table 3, Resting-state studies rows and footnote (p. 216)
key_findings.note: The resting-state pool is not one contrast: by Table 1, three of the ten studies used a baseline rather than a placebo condition and three compared separate groups rather than the same people, so the pooled 'ketamine > placebo' map mixes within-person placebo differences, within-person baseline differences and between-group differences. The moderator test for control condition was null in ten studies, which cannot settle it.

key_findings.finding: Across all 23 task-based studies taken together, no cluster of increased or decreased activation reached significance during acute ketamine administration relative to placebo.
key_findings.locator: Results > Meta-analysis of task-related activity, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Restricted to the 9 executive-function and verbal-fluency studies, ketamine increased activation in the right Heschl's gyrus extending into the right posterior insula (BA 48; 44; -16; 6; Z = 3.306; p < 0.001; 160 voxels), which survived TFCE correction with 142 voxels, and, at the uncorrected threshold only, in the right rostral anterior cingulate and paracingulate gyri (BA 10; 6; 52; 8; Z = 2.889; p < 0.002; 26 voxels).
key_findings.locator: Results > Meta-analysis of task-related activity, 1st paragraph (p. 214); Table 3, Executive functions tasks rows (p. 216)

key_findings.finding: No decrease in activation under ketamine reached significance in any of the three analyses; every cluster reported is an increase.
key_findings.locator: Results > Meta-analysis of resting-state activity and Meta-analysis of task-related activity (p. 214); Table 3 (p. 216)
key_findings.note: The legends of Figures 1 and 2 nevertheless describe the regions as having been impaired by ketamine (pp. 216-217).

key_findings.finding: Heterogeneity was between 0.15% and 6.45% for all results, and Egger's regression tests showed no evidence of publication bias, with all p-values above 0.24.
key_findings.note: Both tests rest on 9 or 10 studies per analysis and are reported only as ranges, without per-cluster values.

key_findings.finding: Every moderator tested was null: for resting-state studies age, sex ratio, dose (bolus and infusion), imaging modality (PET versus fMRI), signal measured, control condition (placebo or baseline) and presence of psychotic-like symptoms; for the executive-function studies age, sex ratio, ketamine type (S versus racemic), psychotic-like symptoms and task impairment.
key_findings.locator: Results > Meta-regression analyses (p. 214, continuing on p. 215)
key_findings.note: Detail is in supplementary tables S3 and S4, which were not read; with 9 to 10 studies these analyses have very little power.

key_findings.finding: Search and selection: 876 articles from PubMed, Web of Science and Google Scholar searched in September 2021, with 11 more from reference lists; 808 abstracts excluded, 79 full texts screened, 46 excluded, 33 articles retained: 10 resting-state (8 fMRI, 2 PET) and 23 task-activation (22 fMRI, 1 PET).

Composition of the pooled literature: the resting-state studies counted 198 participants (75% male, mean age 27.71 years), with three using racemic ketamine, two S-ketamine and five not specifying, and eight of ten assessing psychotomimetic symptoms explicitly; the task studies counted 371 participants (72% male, mean age 27.4 years), with 12 racemic, 7 S-ketamine and 4 unspecified, and 21 of 23 assessing psychotomimetic symptoms. The commonest domains were executive functions and verbal fluency (9 studies), episodic memory (4) and negative emotions (3).
key_findings.note: The 198 is the first column of Table 1 only; the three between-group studies contribute 59 further participants, so the resting-state studies hold 257 people in all (editors' arithmetic from Table 1), which is how the limitations reach n = 628.

key_findings.finding: Study sizes are small: the resting-state studies range from 5 to 34 participants in the ketamine group and the task studies from 8 to 27. The review states its own total as n = 628, with n = 395 in the two analyses that produced results.
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic: 257 (resting-state, both columns) plus 371 (task) = 628; 257 plus the 138 participants of the nine executive-function studies = 395.

key_findings.finding: Of the 19 studies in the two analyses that yielded results, only 8 reported a plasma ketamine level explicitly: mean 98.08 ng/mL, printed as plus or minus 37.68, range 16.6 to 183 ng/mL. The review names the variation and absence of plasma-level information as a limitation, and notes that its own team found higher plasma levels associated with greater acute cognitive impairment.
key_findings.note: The mean is reproducible from the eight values in Tables 1 and 2 (editors' calculation: 98.075), but the printed dispersion is not: the sample standard deviation of those values is 51.12 and the population standard deviation 47.81.

key_findings.finding: The doses used in the included studies lay, as the review describes them, within the therapeutic antidepressant range: on average 0.5 mg/kg over 40 minutes, with a range of 0.1 to 0.75 mg/kg; the introduction gives the psychotomimetic range as bolus doses of 0.1 to 0.26 mg/kg and infusion doses of 0.25 to 0.72 mg/kg per hour.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 2nd paragraph (p. 211); Discussion > Brain activity at rest, last paragraph (p. 218)
key_findings.note: Per-study doses are held in supplementary tables S1 and S2, which were not read, so the two ranges cannot be reconciled from the article.

key_findings.finding: The review states that only one of the 33 included studies used a depression scale and only three used tasks assessing negative emotions, and that most of the included fMRI studies were designed to examine psychotomimetic rather than antidepressant mechanisms; it therefore calls for prudence in reading its results for ketamine's antidepressant action.
key_findings.locator: Discussion > Brain activity at rest, last paragraph (p. 218); Discussion > Limitations, last sentences (p. 219)

reporting_issues.issue: The size of the corrected anterior cingulate cluster is given twice and differently: the Results text says 496 voxels remained after TFCE correction, the footnote of Table 3 says 495.
reporting_issues.consequence: A one-voxel discrepancy of no substantive importance, but a claim quoting the corrected cluster size must name its source; the card uses the table.

reporting_issues.issue: The dispersion printed for the mean plasma level cannot be reproduced from the data in the article: for the eight values in Tables 1 and 2 (16.6, 75, 75, 75, 100, 110, 150, 183 ng/mL) the mean is 98.08 as printed, but the standard deviation is 51.12 (sample) or 47.81 (population), not the 37.68 given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The plasma-level summary should be cited as a mean and range only; the printed plus-or-minus value does not correspond to the tabulated studies (editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: The participant totals are inconsistent between sections: the Results describe the resting-state studies as 198 participants, while the Limitations give a grand total of n = 628, which can only be reached by adding the 59 participants of the second column of Table 1 to the 198 and the 371 of Table 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader comparing the two sections cannot reconcile them; any claim about how many people the meta-analysis rests on must say whether the comparison groups of the three between-group studies are counted.

reporting_issues.issue: The TOTAL row of Table 1 mixes two bases: its mean age of 27.71 years is reproduced only by weighting across all 257 resting-state participants, including the comparison groups of the three between-group studies (weighting across the 198 the text names gives 27.61 and the unweighted study-level mean is 27.45), while its figure of 0.75 for the share of men is the unweighted mean of the ten study-level proportions (weighting across the 198 gives 0.69 and across all 257 gives 0.66). The row of Table 2 is consistent either way for the sex ratio (0.72) and its mean age of 27.4 is the participant-weighted value, the unweighted being 27.8. All figures are editors' calculations from the printed rows.
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline '75% were male' for the resting-state studies describes the average study, not the pooled participants, in whom the share is about 66%, and the age and sex figures in the same row do not rest on the same base; a claim quoting either should say which.

reporting_issues.issue: The column reporting the share of men is headed 'm/f ratio' in Table 1 and 'm/n ratio' in Table 2, while the text reads the same figures as a percentage of men; a value of 1 is used for all-male samples, which is a proportion of the sample, not a male-to-female ratio.
reporting_issues.consequence: The Table 1 heading is wrong; the values are proportions of men, as the text's reading and the all-male studies show.

reporting_issues.issue: The legends of Figures 1 and 2 state that the figures display brain regions that were impaired by ketamine relative to placebo, while every result in Table 3 and in the text is an increase in activation; the same legends note that the threshold was lowered to obtain better graphic results for the clusters that did not survive correction.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figures cannot be cited for impairment of any region, and the pictures show clusters drawn at a threshold lower than the one that produced them; claims should use Table 3 with its thresholds.

reporting_issues.issue: The list of moderators tested does not match between Methods and Results for the resting-state analysis: the Methods name ketamine type and do not name dose, while the Results report dose (bolus and infusion) and do not report ketamine type.
reporting_issues.consequence: It cannot be determined from the article whether ketamine type was tested as a moderator of the resting-state results, which matters because racemic and S-ketamine were both used and five of the ten studies did not specify the type.

reporting_issues.issue: The correction method is written as TFCE in the Methods and abstract and as TCFE in the Discussion and in the Table 3 footnote.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; threshold-free cluster enhancement is meant throughout.

reporting_issues.issue: The enumerations in the Methods are broken: the selection criteria run (i), (ii), (iii), (iiii), (iv), (v), (vi), and the data-extraction list runs (i) to (x) and then jumps to (xiv) and (xv).
reporting_issues.consequence: Typesetting only, but it leaves open whether extraction items (xi) to (xiii) existed and were dropped from the printed list.

reporting_issues.issue: Heterogeneity and publication-bias results are reported only as ranges across all significant clusters (I-squared 0.15% to 6.45%; Egger's p above 0.24), with no per-cluster values, and the power of these tests with 9 or 10 studies is not discussed.
reporting_issues.consequence: A claim cannot state heterogeneity or publication bias for a particular cluster, and the reassurance these statistics appear to give should not be carried into the encyclopedia's wording.

reporting_issues.issue: Four of the nine executive-function studies may not be independent samples. In Table 2 Daumann et al. (2008) and Daumann et al. (2010) share every printed characteristic (n = 14, mean age 32.1, sex ratio 0.57, S-ketamine, executive functions) and Nagels et al. (2011) and Nagels et al. (2018) likewise (n = 15, mean age 27, sex ratio 1, S-ketamine); Honey et al. appears three times across Tables 1 and 2. The review never says whether these are separate datasets, and the pooling method treats them as independent.
reporting_issues.consequence: If either pair is one dataset analysed twice, the nine studies and 138 participants behind the corrected executive-function cluster are fewer than they look, and METHODS 6.3 would not count such pairs as independent replication; any claim citing the number of studies should carry this caution.

reporting_issues.issue: The literature was searched in September 2021 (p. 212) and the article was received in September 2022, accepted in February 2023 and printed with a 2024 journal year, so the evidence base is about two and a half years older than the citation year suggests.
reporting_issues.consequence: A claim dated 2024 that rests on this review should say when the search closed; studies published after September 2021 are not in it.
